title: REG U4·W3 — Business Law I: Contracts, UCC Sales & Agency
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the legal backbone of a construction deal

Every MBG project rests on contracts — with the owner, the subcontractors, and the material suppliers — and on the agents who sign them. REG tests business law alongside tax, and this week covers the law of contracts (common law), the UCC Article 2 rules that govern the sale of goods, and the agency doctrines that decide who is bound when an employee or officer acts. These are the rules that make a handshake — or a purchase order — enforceable.

Contract formation

A valid contract requires an offer, an acceptance, and consideration (a bargained-for exchange of legal value), plus capacity and a legal purpose. An offer shows present intent and definite terms; it can be revoked any time before acceptance unless an exception holds it open. Acceptance must generally mirror the offer under common law (the mirror-image rule), and under the mailbox rule an acceptance is effective when dispatched. Consideration must be new — past consideration and a pre-existing duty do not count.

Defenses to formation and enforcement

Even a formed contract may be void or voidable. Defenses include lack of capacity (a minor's contract is voidable by the minor), duress, undue influence, fraud or misrepresentation, mutual mistake, and illegality. The Statute of Frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing and signed by the party to be charged: contracts for an interest in land, those that cannot be performed within one year, a suretyship (promise to pay another's debt), and — under the UCC — sales of goods of $500 or more. The parol evidence rule then bars prior or contemporaneous oral terms that contradict a final written contract.

Performance, breach, and remedies

Common-law contracts require substantial performance; a material breach excuses the non-breaching party and triggers remedies. The usual remedy is compensatory damages (the benefit of the bargain), plus consequential damages that were foreseeable. Specific performance is available only for unique subject matter (real estate, rare goods) — not personal services. Liquidated-damages clauses are enforceable if the amount was a reasonable estimate and not a penalty, and the non-breaching party must mitigate its losses. These remedies aim to put the injured party where performance would have.

UCC Article 2 — sale of goods

The UCC Article 2 governs contracts for the sale of goods (movable, tangible things) and relaxes several common-law rules, with extra duties for merchants. A merchant's signed firm offer stays open without consideration for the stated time (up to three months). Article 2 also abandons the mirror-image rule: under the battle of the forms (§2-207), an acceptance with additional terms can still form a contract, and between merchants those terms may become part of the deal unless they materially alter it, are objected to, or the offer limited acceptance. A contract can form even with open terms if the parties intended to contract.

Risk of loss and warranties

Article 2 allocates risk of loss. In a shipment contract (FOB seller's location) risk passes to the buyer when the seller delivers to the carrier; in a destination contract (FOB buyer's location) risk passes on tender at the destination. Goods carry warranties: an express warranty from an affirmation or sample; the implied warranty of merchantability (goods are fit for ordinary use — given automatically by a merchant seller); and the implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose when the seller knows the buyer is relying on the seller to select suitable goods. The perfect-tender rule lets a buyer reject goods that fail to conform in any respect, subject to the seller's right to cure.

Agency — authority

An agency is a relationship in which an agent acts on behalf of a principal. An agent can bind the principal through actual authority — express (stated) or implied (reasonably necessary to carry out the express authority) — or through apparent authority, created by the principal's conduct toward the third party that reasonably leads the third party to believe the agent is authorized. Ratification can bind a principal to an unauthorized act done on its behalf if the principal later approves it with knowledge of the facts. Apparent authority is why MBG must be careful about what its job superintendents appear empowered to sign.

Agency — liability and duties

Whether the principal and agent are liable on a contract depends on disclosure. For a disclosed principal (the third party knows who it is), the principal is liable and the agent generally is not. For a partially disclosed (identity unknown) or undisclosed principal, both the agent and the principal can be held liable. The agent owes the principal fiduciary duties — loyalty, obedience, care, and accounting — and the principal owes the agent compensation and reimbursement. In tort, a principal is liable under respondeat superior for an employee's torts committed within the scope of employment.

Discharge, assignment, and third-party rights

Contract obligations can end other than by performance. A contract is discharged by accord and satisfaction (agreeing to and rendering a substitute performance), by novation (substituting a new party with everyone's consent), by impossibility or impracticability, or by mutual rescission. Rights can be assigned and duties delegated — though duties involving personal skill or that materially change the obligee's risk cannot be delegated. A third-party beneficiary who was intended to benefit (not merely an incidental beneficiary) can enforce the contract. A party who learns of an anticipatory repudiation — the other side's clear statement that it will not perform — may treat the contract as breached immediately and sue without waiting for the performance date. These doctrines decide who, beyond the original two parties, can sue or be released on a deal.

CMA bridge

MBG's purchase orders for lumber and steel are UCC Article 2 contracts; its agreements with the owner and subcontractors are common-law construction contracts; and the authority of its project managers to bind the company is pure agency law. The CFO who understands which body of law governs a document — and who is authorized to sign it — manages real legal and cash-flow risk.

Practice and recap

  1. Form a contract (offer + acceptance + consideration); apply the mirror-image and mailbox rules under common law.
  2. Spot defenses and the Statute of Frauds writing requirements (land, >1 year, suretyship, goods ≥$500); apply the parol evidence rule.
  3. Apply UCC Article 2 for goods: merchant firm offer, battle of the forms (§2-207), risk of loss (shipment vs destination), warranties, perfect tender.
  4. Analyze agency: actual (express/implied) vs apparent authority, ratification, disclosed/undisclosed principal liability, fiduciary duties, respondeat superior.

Recap: a contract needs offer, acceptance, and consideration, with common law using the mirror-image and mailbox rules and the Statute of Frauds requiring writings for land, >1-year, suretyship, and ≥$500 goods contracts; UCC Article 2 governs goods with merchant firm offers, the §2-207 battle of the forms, shipment-vs-destination risk of loss, merchantability/fitness warranties, and perfect tender; and agency binds a principal through actual or apparent authority, with disclosed principals liable (agent not) and undisclosed principals leaving both exposed, all under the agent's fiduciary duties.

flashcards.back: Offer + acceptance + consideration (bargained-for legal value), plus capacity and legality. Past consideration and pre-existing duty are not valid consideration.
Mailbox: acceptance effective when dispatched. Mirror-image (common law): acceptance must match the offer exactly. UCC relaxes mirror-image via §2-207.
Land interests, contracts not performable within 1 year, suretyship (promise to pay another's debt), and UCC sales of goods ≥ $500.
A merchant's signed written offer stays open without consideration for the time stated, up to 3 months.
An acceptance with additional terms can still form a contract; between merchants, additional terms join unless they materially alter, are objected to, or the offer limited acceptance.
Shipment contract (FOB seller): risk passes when goods given to the carrier. Destination contract (FOB buyer): risk passes on tender at destination.
Merchantability (fit for ordinary use — automatic from a merchant seller); fitness for a particular purpose (seller knows buyer relies on seller to select goods).

Actual = express or implied authority the principal gives the agent. Apparent = principal's conduct toward a third party makes the agent appear authorized. Disclosed principal liable; undisclosed → both liable.

questions.q: Under the Statute of Frauds, which contract must be in writing?
choices: A sale of goods for $500 or more
An oral agreement to lend a tool
questions.explain: UCC requires a writing for sales of goods of $500 or more; land, >1-year, and suretyship contracts also require writings.

questions.q: A merchant's signed written firm offer stays open without consideration for up to:
questions.explain: A UCC firm offer is irrevocable for the stated time, up to 3 months, without consideration.

questions.q: In a shipment contract (FOB seller's location), risk of loss passes to the buyer when:
choices: The seller delivers the goods to the carrier
questions.explain: In a shipment contract risk passes when conforming goods are delivered to the carrier.

questions.q: The implied warranty of merchantability is given automatically by:
choices: A merchant seller of goods of that kind
questions.explain: Merchantability is implied whenever the seller is a merchant who deals in goods of that kind.

choices: The principal's conduct toward the third party
questions.explain: Apparent authority arises from the principal's manifestations to the third party, not the agent's own statements.

questions.q: When a principal is UNDISCLOSED, liability on the contract falls on:
choices: Both the agent and the principal
questions.explain: With an undisclosed (or partially disclosed) principal, both the agent and the principal can be liable.

questions.q: Specific performance is generally available for:
choices: Unique subject matter such as real estate
questions.explain: Specific performance applies to unique goods or real estate; courts will not order personal services.
